prompts.prompt:
<role>
You're making the reel a studio watches before deciding whether to hire you. It has to sell your craft within its opening seconds.
</role>

<spec>
- Duration: {{length}} seconds
- Frame: {{size}}, 60 fps
- Tempo: {{bpm}} BPM
- Type: {{typeface}}, two weights at most
- Color: {{palette}}
- Idea: {{concept}}
</spec>

<thread>
Before designing, reduce the idea to one sentence. Then choose a carrier (a glyph, a shape or a stroke) that stays visible in every act and physically turns into the next one. Hard cuts and dissolves are off the table: the carrier is the only way from one act to another.
</thread>

<acts>
Divide the running time into five acts of about equal length:
- Act 1, type: letters spell out the idea, then gather, split and reflow.
- Act 2, shape: the carrier steps through a few geometric forms.
- Act 3, depth: the layout tilts off the flat plane and the camera flies into it.
- Act 4, data: a graph or a UI panel builds up piece by piece and comes to rest.
- Act 5, sign-off: everything folds back into the carrier, then a title card.
Each visible change starts exactly on a beat. Save the strongest hit for the first beat of the final bar, and make the closing frame match the opening one so the reel loops.
</acts>

<rules>
Solid color planes with sharp edges. Build depth out of scale, overlap and parallax; leave out shadows and glows.
Steer clear of everything that makes motion look machine-made: lens flares, bloom, exploding particles, chromatic fringing, shaky cameras, wallpaper gradients, rubbery overshoot, captions stuck in a corner.
</rules>

<pipeline>
1. Build one HTML page around a single frame(t) function. Every property is derived from t alone, with no CSS animation, no timers and nothing remembered from the previous frame, so frames can be rendered in any order.
2. Write the easing by hand: critically damped springs where things settle, exponential curves for fast travel, and blur along the direction of motion for anything fast.
3. Synthesize the soundtrack with an OfflineAudioContext: a kick under each beat, filtered noise rising into the final bar, a short impact at every act change. Save it to a WAV file.
4. Step through the timeline in Playwright, 60 frames per second, average three subframes per output frame (ffmpeg's tmix filter) for motion blur, and mux the WAV into the result.
</pipeline>

<check>
Before the final render, lay out one still per beat on a single contact sheet. Correct whatever is cramped, early or late against the beat, colliding or illegible. Only then render.
</check>

<reply>
Open with the idea, the carrier and a storyboard that goes beat by beat. After that, build the whole thing with no more questions and send me the finished MP4.
</reply>

<facts>
- Product: {{product}}
- What it does: {{pitch}}
- Show these features: {{features}}
If anything on this list is missing, check with me first. Do not invent anything about the product.
</facts>

<format>
Length: {{length}} seconds. Frame: {{size}}. Brand colors: {{colors}}. Font: {{typeface}}.
</format>

<interface>
Recreate the product's actual interface as layered HTML (no screenshots), so every panel, control and number can be animated. Whenever the interface is at rest, it sits at exact 1:1 pixels and stays sharp.
Keep on-screen text to seven words or fewer at a time, and leave each line up long enough to be read twice.
Skip: canned background gradients, phones floating in 3D, made-up dashboards stuffed with fake numbers, lens flares and particles.
</interface>

<beats>
Shares of the running time are approximate:
- Opening, roughly a tenth: one short animated line naming the problem.
- Reveal, roughly 15 percent: that line breaks apart and becomes the product's interface.
- Features, roughly 60 percent: one section per feature, each demonstrated rather than described. A pointer clicks, drags or types, the UI answers, and the camera leans in on the detail that matters before easing back.
- Close, roughly 15 percent: the name or logo, followed by {{ending}}.
Sections flow into each other through continuous transitions (a panel turns into the next screen), never a hard cut.
</beats>

<engineering>
1. A single HTML page where frame(t) computes every value from t. Skip CSS keyframes and timers, so frames can be produced in any order.
2. Spring physics for UI elements, exponential curves for camera travel, blur on anything moving fast.
3. Generate a light soundtrack in code: a 110 to 120 BPM pulse, soft ticks under pointer actions, an accent when the closing card lands. Write it out as WAV.
4. Record at 60 fps through Playwright, encode the frames with ffmpeg and add the audio track.
</engineering>

<proof>
Before anything else, export a still from every section. Make sure every word is legible, the UI is recognisably the real product and no elements collide, then render the full video.
</proof>

<answer>
Read the facts back to me with a brief shot list to confirm, then go ahead and build it without checking in again, and send the MP4.
</answer>

<intent>
Create {{length}} seconds of real-time 3D in three.js at {{size}}, built around a single subject: {{subject}}. It should have the calm of a studio product film rather than the clutter of a tech demo.
</intent>

<camera-and-light>
- Light: {{lighting}}. PBR materials whose roughness and reflections feel believable; use an HDR environment map for reflections only.
- Color: {{palette}}.
- Lens: keep one focal length throughout, near 50 mm. Narrow focus on close shots, plus a fine layer of grain.
- Movement: treat the camera as if it sits on a dolly or a crane. Slow pushes and lifts that ease in and out; never a free orbit.
- Leave out: glow smeared over every surface, neon wire meshes, starry backdrops, aimless particles, and circling the subject for no reason.
</camera-and-light>

<arc>
Three movements, in this order:
1. Emerge: the subject comes out of darkness or assembles from its parts.
2. Change: it shifts state in one unbroken motion (it unfolds, assembles, melts or rearranges).
3. Hold: the camera settles on a slow hero view, then drifts back to where it began so the last frame flows into the first.
</arc>

<engineering>
1. Derive every transform and material parameter from time inside frame(t). Seed each simulation and advance it in fixed steps, so a given frame number always produces the same image.
2. Go light on post-processing: tone mapping, a depth-of-field pass, some grain. Bloom belongs only on materials that actually emit light.
3. Render offline rather than by screen capture: call frame(t) from Playwright for every 1/60 s, grab the canvas pixels, and have ffmpeg encode H.264 in yuv420p.
</engineering>

<proof>
First export five stills spaced evenly through the piece and check each at 100% zoom. Clean up jagged edges, grainy shadows, clipped highlights and any surface that looks like a default material. Only then render the video.
</proof>

<answer>
Sum up the subject, the three movements and where the camera travels in a short note, then build it with no further questions and send the MP4.
</answer>
